title: Battery Backup for CPAP (2026): 7 Picks Sized by Nights of Use
metaDescription: The EcoFlow River 3 Plus is the best CPAP battery backup for most; a 288Wh station on DC runs a 25-watt CPAP about 10 hours. 7 picks, plus FAA battery rules.
h1: The 7 Best Battery Backups for CPAP in 2026
intro:
Seven batteries that keep a CPAP running through an outage, a camping trip or a flight, with the humidifier wattage and runtime math that decide which size you need.

A CPAP barely sips power until you turn on the heated humidifier. Size the battery for the settings you will actually sleep with, and the right pick becomes obvious.
quickAnswer: the EcoFlow River 3 Plus Portable Power Station is our #1 pick (best overall for cpap). The right size for most CPAP users: a quiet bedside UPS at home that doubles as a one-to-two-night camping battery.
picksHeading: The 7 Best Battery Backups for CPAP in 2026, Ranked

picks.body: The River 3 Plus is the size class most CPAP users should start with. EcoFlow rates it at about 286 watt-hours of LFP storage with 600 watts of AC output, so the inverter has enormous headroom over any CPAP and its humidifier. EcoFlow also lists an EPS (emergency power supply) mode with a switchover it rates at under 10 milliseconds, which is what lets it sit between the wall and the machine and take over during an outage without waking you. By the runtime math in this guide, a machine drawing 25 watts without humidification gets roughly 9 to 10 hours from the battery through a DC converter, about one full night with margin; turn on a heated humidifier and heated tube and that can shrink to a few hours. EcoFlow sells an extra battery that clips on and raises capacity substantially, which turns it into a multi-night camping unit. It is not airline-legal, so frequent flyers need a dedicated pack as well.
pros: Roughly 286Wh of LFP covers one to two humidifier-free nights
Fast-switching EPS mode suits a bedside UPS role
12V car-style port for a CPAP maker's DC converter
Add-on battery can roughly triple capacity later
Light enough to carry to the bedroom or campsite
cons: Heated humidifier plus heated tube can drain it in a single night
Too heavy and too large to carry on a plane
Add-on battery costs extra and adds weight

picks.body: Medistrom builds the Pilot-24 Lite specifically for CPAP machines, and its main selling point is a capacity rated just under the 100 watt-hour line that most airlines and the FAA treat as the no-paperwork limit for carry-on lithium batteries. It outputs DC directly, so there is no inverter wasting a slice of the battery, and it uses a cable matched to your machine model, so check the compatibility list for your exact CPAP before buying. How long it lasts depends heavily on your draw: at low pressures with humidification and heated tubing off, some machines sip little enough for a full night, while at an average of 25 watts the math works out to about three and a half hours, so measure before you trust it. Medistrom also makes a 12-volt version, the Pilot-12 Lite, for machines that run on 12V; buying the wrong one is the most common mistake. Two Pilot-24 Lite packs are still airline-legal as spares in most cases, which is the cleanest way to cover a two-night trip.
pros: Rated just under 100Wh, so no airline approval is needed
DC output avoids inverter losses entirely
Small enough to pack in a CPAP travel bag
Model-specific cables for widely used ResMed and Philips machines
USB port for a phone in the tent or hotel
cons: A full night is realistic only at low draw with the humidifier off
Requires the correct machine-specific cable, sold separately for some models
Expensive per watt-hour compared with a power station

picks.body: Jackery's Explorer 300 Plus is a small LFP station with about 288 watt-hours of storage and a 300-watt inverter, according to Jackery's published specs, in a body that weighs roughly 8 pounds. For a CPAP that is all the output you need, even with a heated humidifier running, and the capacity puts it in the same one-to-two-night class as the River 3 Plus. Its 12V car-style socket is the better way to power a CPAP: plug in your machine maker's DC converter or a compatible DC cable and skip the inverter losses entirely. It does not expand, so if you think you will want three or four nights off-grid, a larger station is the smarter buy. For a weekend camping trip where you charge it full at home and maybe top it up from a folding panel or the car, it is about as simple as a CPAP battery gets. Confirm any UPS or pass-through behavior on Jackery's current spec sheet before relying on it as a bedside backup.
pros: About 288Wh of LFP in a compact, carry-handle body
300W inverter is plenty for any CPAP and humidifier
12V car-style output for a DC converter
Simple controls with little to configure
cons: Not expandable
300W limit rules out most other bedside appliances
Like any 288Wh station, it is too large to fly with

picks.body: Anker's SOLIX C300 is another 288 watt-hour LFP station with a 300-watt AC inverter, and its strength is the USB-C side: Anker rates its top USB-C port at 140 watts, enough to charge most laptops at full speed while a CPAP runs from the 12V or AC output. That makes it a good fit for travel nurses, van campers and anyone whose overnight load is a CPAP plus a laptop and phone. It can also recharge over USB-C, which means a powerful laptop-style charger or a car USB-C adapter can top it up without the proprietary brick. Capacity is the same one-to-two-night class as the other small stations here, and the same caveats apply: humidifier on, expect a single night or less; humidifier off on a DC converter, expect a night with margin. Anker also sells DC-only variants of this family; if you want to plug the CPAP's standard power brick in, make sure the version you buy has AC outlets.
pros: About 288Wh of LFP in a compact upright body
Strong USB-C output for laptops and phones alongside the CPAP
12V car-style output for a DC converter
Recharges from USB-C as well as solar and car
cons: 300W AC is the ceiling
Not expandable
Too large to carry on a plane

picks.body: If your outages tend to last more than a night, or you want the CPAP battery to keep a phone, lamp and fan going too, step up to the kilowatt-hour class. Jackery rates the Explorer 1000 v2 at 1,070 watt-hours of LFP and 1,500 watts continuous with a 3,000-watt surge, in a body of roughly 24 pounds. For a CPAP alone that is multiple nights: a 30-watt draw through the 12V port should run somewhere around 30 hours of sleep by the efficiency math in this guide, and even with a heated humidifier pulling 60 watts you are looking at two to three nights. The output is high enough to run a refrigerator during the day, which matters in a long outage. The trade-off is that it is far more battery than a weekend camper needs, and at roughly three times the weight of the 288Wh units it is not something you casually carry to a tent site. Check Jackery's current listing for its UPS switchover specification.
pros: About 1,070Wh covers several nights even with some humidification
1,500W output also runs a fridge or fan in the day
Light for its capacity at about 24 pounds
Fast AC recharge between nights when power returns briefly
cons: Overkill and heavy for CPAP-only camping
Not expandable
Costs several times as much as a 288Wh station

picks.award: Best Bedside UPS for Long Outages
picks.body: The Delta 3 Plus is the kilowatt-hour station to choose if the job is primarily an always-on bedside UPS. EcoFlow rates it at 1,024 watt-hours of LFP, 1,800 watts continuous, and an EPS switchover of 10 milliseconds, which is fast enough that a CPAP plugged into it should not notice the grid dropping out. Leave it plugged in at the bedside, plug the CPAP into it, and an outage at 3 a.m. becomes a non-event. Capacity covers several nights with the humidifier off and a couple with it on, and EcoFlow's expansion batteries can extend that if you live where outages last a week. During the day the 1,800-watt inverter can run a refrigerator, which makes it a genuine home-backup tool rather than a single-purpose CPAP battery. Two cautions: fast charging spins up the fan, so set a slower charge rate in the app if it sits in the bedroom, and it is too heavy to be a convenient camping companion.
pros: About 1kWh of LFP covers several CPAP nights
EcoFlow-rated 10ms EPS switchover for seamless bedside backup
Expandable with extra batteries
1,800W output handles a fridge or space fan during the day
Fast wall charging
cons: Around 28 pounds; it lives at home, not in a tent
More expensive than the Jackery 1000 v2 at many retailers
Fan noise during fast charging in a bedroom

picks.body: If you are searching for the best generator for a CPAP machine, the honest answer is that a generator should usually charge the battery that runs the CPAP, not run the machine directly through the night. With that framing, the Honda EU2200i is the benchmark. Honda rates it at 2,200 starting and 1,800 running watts, and as an inverter generator its output is clean enough for electronics like a CPAP power supply and a power station's charger. It is quiet for a gas generator, but it is still a combustion engine that produces carbon monoxide: it must run outdoors, well away from doors, windows and vents, with CO alarms inside. The smart routine is to run it for a few hours in the afternoon to recharge a power station and the fridge, then shut it down and let the battery carry the CPAP silently overnight. Running a 1,800-watt engine all night for a 30-watt machine is a poor use of fuel.
pros: Inverter output is suitable for sensitive electronics
Among the quietest gas generators in its class
Runs a CPAP plus a fridge or window fan
Recharges a power station during the day
Long reputation for reliability and parts support
cons: Must run outdoors, far from windows, never in a garage or tent
Gas storage and maintenance
Running it all night for a 30W load is wasteful and noisy for neighbors

sections.heading: The Short Answer: What Size Battery Your CPAP Needs
sections.body:
A CPAP is one of the easiest medical devices to back up with a battery, and also one of the easiest to get wrong. The machine itself is frugal; the heated humidifier and heated tube are not. A battery that comfortably covers two nights with humidification off may not make it to dawn with everything on, and that difference is what decides whether you need a 99 watt-hour travel pack, a 288 watt-hour camping station or a kilowatt-hour box beside the bed.

This guide covers both kinds of battery backup for CPAP users. Dedicated CPAP batteries like the Medistrom Pilot-24 Lite are small, airline-friendly and output DC straight to the machine. Portable power stations like the EcoFlow River 3 Plus and Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 are bigger lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries with AC outlets, 12V sockets and USB, and some of them can sit between the wall and the CPAP as an uninterruptible power supply. If you want the wider picture first, our [portable power station rankings](/best-portable-power-station/) cover the general-purpose units these picks are drawn from.

THE SHORT ANSWER

For most people, a roughly 300Wh LFP station with a 12V DC cable is the right first CPAP battery.

It covers one to two nights with the humidifier off, works as a bedside backup, and doubles as a camping battery. Fly often? Add a sub-100Wh dedicated pack. Long outages? Step up to a 1kWh station.

Before anything else: this is a buying guide, not medical advice. Your CPAP manufacturer publishes approved power accessories, and your durable medical equipment (DME) supplier and doctor should confirm that a given battery or DC cable is suitable for your machine and prescription. None of the power stations here is a medical device or medically certified, and none of them changes what your machine is approved to do. What they change is whether your therapy stops when the power does.

The picks below are described from manufacturers' published specifications and the runtime math later in this guide, not from hands-on testing. Every runtime figure is an estimate. Your pressure setting, mask leak, humidifier level, room temperature and machine model all move the real number, which is why the most useful thing in this article is the method for calculating your own nights of runtime, not any single headline figure.

sections.heading: How Many Watts a CPAP Uses, With and Without the Humidifier
sections.body:
The number printed on your CPAP's power brick is not what it uses. That label is the maximum the supply can deliver, and on popular machines such as the ResMed AirSense series it is typically 90 watts. Actual draw is far lower most of the night. The blower motor at typical pressures uses a modest amount; what pushes consumption up is the heating element in the humidifier tub and, if you use one, the heated tube. Those heaters can easily double or triple the machine's average draw, especially in a cold bedroom.

As a planning range, many modern CPAP machines average somewhere around 15 to 40 watts with humidification and heated tubing switched off, depending on pressure. With a heated humidifier and heated tube running, plan for roughly 50 to 90 watts, with the high end in cold rooms and at high humidity settings. BiPAP and auto-adjusting machines at high pressures sit toward the top of each range. These are broad bands for sizing, not a spec for your machine.

| Setup | Planning draw | Energy per 8-hour night |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CPAP, humidifier and heated tube off | 15-40W | 120-320Wh |
| CPAP, humidifier on, standard tube | 40-70W | 320-560Wh |
| CPAP, humidifier and heated tube on | 50-90W | 400-720Wh |
| BiPAP at high pressure, full humidification | 60-100W+ | 480-800Wh+ |

The best way to get your real number is to measure it. A plug-in watt meter between the wall and the CPAP's power brick will show average watts and total watt-hours over a night, and those meters are inexpensive. Run one for two or three nights with your normal settings, then once with the humidifier off. The difference tells you exactly how much battery the humidifier costs you, which is the single most important number in this whole decision. Some machines also report usage data in their app, but a meter at the wall captures the power brick's own losses too.

Most people who rely on a battery end up turning the humidifier down or off on battery nights. That is a comfort trade-off, not a requirement, and it is worth asking your doctor or sleep clinic whether a night or two without heated humidification is acceptable for you. If it is not, plan for a bigger battery rather than hoping a small one stretches. A battery that dies at 3 a.m. is worse than a heavier battery that makes it to morning.

sections.heading: DC Cable vs AC Inverter: The Free Runtime Most People Miss
sections.body:
Every portable power station stores energy as DC and has to convert it to 120-volt AC through an inverter to power a standard wall plug. Your CPAP's power brick then converts that AC back to the low-voltage DC the machine actually runs on. Each conversion wastes energy as heat, and the inverter also draws its own idle power just from being switched on. Together, running a CPAP on AC from a battery often loses something like 10 to 20 percent of the battery compared with powering it directly on DC.

The fix is a DC converter or cable. ResMed, Philips and other manufacturers sell DC power accessories for their machines that plug into a 12V car-style socket, and battery makers like Medistrom sell model-specific cables for their packs. Plug that into the 12V output of a power station and the station's inverter never turns on. On a small 288Wh station, that saving alone can be the difference between one night and a night and a half.

WORTH KNOWING

DC power often disables or limits the heated humidifier.

Some machines restrict humidifier heating when running from a DC converter or battery to conserve power. Check your manual. If you rely on heated humidification, you may have to use AC from the power station anyway, and size the battery for it.

Compatibility is where the details matter. ResMed AirSense machines run on a 24-volt supply, so they need a converter that steps up from 12V or a battery with a native 24V output, such as the Pilot-24 Lite. Some other machines run on 12V and use a different cable or a different battery model entirely. Buying the right battery with the wrong cable is the most common and most avoidable CPAP battery mistake. Take your machine's exact model name to the battery maker's compatibility chart, or ask your DME supplier, before ordering anything.

If you do run on AC, use a station with a pure sine wave inverter, which every station on this list has, and plug the CPAP's own power brick in rather than a cheap universal adapter. Turn off any other AC loads you do not need so the inverter is not working harder than necessary, and switch the inverter off in the morning. An inverter left idling with nothing plugged in can quietly eat a meaningful slice of a small battery over a day.

sections.heading: Nights of Runtime: The Math, Worked Out
sections.body:
Runtime math for a CPAP battery is simple once you have the average watts. Take the battery's rated watt-hours, multiply by an efficiency factor, and divide by the CPAP's average draw. Use roughly 0.85 if you are running through the AC inverter and roughly 0.9 if you are running a DC cable from the 12V port. That gives you hours of runtime. Divide by the hours you sleep to get nights.

A worked example: a 288Wh station on DC, powering a machine that averages 25 watts with the humidifier off, gives 288 times 0.9, or about 259 usable watt-hours, divided by 25 watts, or about 10 hours. That is one full night with a little margin. Switch to AC with the humidifier on at 60 watts and the same battery gives 288 times 0.85, or about 245 watt-hours, divided by 60, which is about 4 hours. That is the same battery, two completely different answers.

| Battery | DC, 25W (humidifier off) | AC, 60W (humidifier on) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 99Wh dedicated CPAP pack | ~3.5 hours (bigger with low pressure) | Not recommended |
| 286-288Wh station | ~10 hours / about 1 night | ~4 hours |
| ~1,000-1,070Wh station | ~36-38 hours / 4+ nights | ~14-15 hours / about 2 nights |
| Two-battery expanded station | Several more nights | Several more nights |

Dedicated CPAP packs like the Pilot-24 Lite are typically marketed with longer per-night figures than this table suggests, because battery makers assume low pressure settings and no humidification, and some machines draw well under 25 watts in those conditions. That is a reasonable claim for those conditions; just do not assume it applies to you until you have measured your own draw. The table also ignores the cold: lithium batteries deliver less capacity in a freezing tent, so add margin for winter camping.

A useful rule: buy a battery with at least 1.5 times the capacity your math says you need for the nights you want to cover. Batteries lose a little capacity with age, your mask may leak more one night than another, and the cost of running out is waking up without therapy. If the math says one night on a 288Wh station, treat that station as a one-night battery, not a two-night battery, and plan a recharge between nights.

sections.heading: Flying With a CPAP Battery: The 100Wh and 160Wh Rules
sections.body:
Air travel is where dedicated CPAP batteries earn their price. Under FAA and common airline rules for passengers, spare lithium-ion batteries must go in carry-on bags, never checked luggage. Batteries rated at 100 watt-hours or less are generally allowed without airline approval. Batteries between 100 and 160 watt-hours need airline approval and are usually limited to two spares per passenger. Lithium batteries over 160 watt-hours are not permitted on passenger aircraft at all.

That last line rules out every portable power station on this list. A 286Wh River 3 Plus or 288Wh Explorer 300 Plus cannot fly, regardless of the fact that you need it for a medical device. This is why the Pilot-24 Lite exists: it is rated just under 100Wh specifically so that it falls into the simplest category. Check that the watt-hour rating is printed on the battery itself, because security screeners may ask, and an unlabeled pack can be refused.

BEFORE YOU FLY

Check your airline's own battery and medical-device policy, not just the FAA rule.

Airlines can be stricter than the baseline, some require advance notice for using a CPAP onboard, and international carriers follow their own regulators. Carry a copy of your machine's manual page on battery use and a note from your doctor.

If you intend to use the CPAP in flight, which some long-haul travelers do, the airline typically requires that the battery can run the device for longer than the flight duration with a margin, and some want advance notice through their medical or special-assistance desk. Using a CPAP onboard is usually done with humidification off. Airlines also commonly look for a manufacturer label stating the machine meets FAA requirements for in-flight use; most mainstream CPAPs carry one, but verify for your model before the trip.

For a two-night trip with no reliable power, two sub-100Wh packs are usually the cleanest solution: both remain in the no-approval category, each can cover much or all of a night at low pressure with humidification off, and you can recharge both at the destination. A travel CPAP such as the ResMed AirMini is designed with this kind of trip in mind and pairs with compact batteries, but whether a travel machine suits your prescription is a question for your doctor, not a battery guide.

sections.heading: Camping With a CPAP: A Portable Setup That Works
sections.body:
A portable CPAP setup for camping is mostly a capacity-and-recharge plan. The battery has to cover each night, and something has to put energy back during the day. For a weekend, a fully charged 288Wh station with a DC cable and the humidifier off covers the first night and much of the second. For anything longer, you need a way to recharge: a folding solar panel, a car's 12V outlet while driving, or a campground hookup.

Solar is the natural partner. A 100-watt folding panel aimed well on a clear summer day can put back very roughly 300 to 500 watt-hours, which refills a 288Wh station; on an overcast day, plan on a fraction of that. Our guides to the [best power stations for camping](/best-portable-power-station-for-camping/) and [best portable solar panels](/best-portable-solar-panel/) cover pairings, and the [solar generator guide](/best-solar-generator/) walks through the sun-hours math in detail. Keep the battery in the tent or vehicle overnight, not outside in the cold, and move it into the shade during the day.

Drive-in campers can also charge from the car. Most stations accept 12V car charging, though at a modest rate, so a few hours of driving puts back a partial charge rather than a full one. Never idle a vehicle near a tent to charge a battery: exhaust carbon monoxide is just as dangerous from a car as from a generator. If you are at a site with a generator, our guide to the [best generators for camping](/best-generator-for-camping/) covers quiet models, but follow the same rule as at home: let the generator charge the battery during the day and let the battery run the CPAP overnight.

Pack a backup. That means the DC cable and the CPAP's own AC brick, distilled water if you use a humidifier, and a plan for a night if the battery comes up short. Many experienced campers bring a second small battery, and for backpacking, where every ounce counts, a single sub-100Wh dedicated pack and a humidifier-off night is the realistic ceiling. Test the full setup at home on battery for a night before you leave, so the first failure happens in your bedroom and not at a trailhead.

sections.heading: UPS Mode: A Bedside Backup That Never Wakes You
sections.body:
At home, the most valuable thing a power station can do for a CPAP user is act as an uninterruptible power supply. Plug the station into the wall, plug the CPAP into the station, and the station passes grid power through to the machine. When the grid fails, the station switches to its battery fast enough that the CPAP should keep running. Without that, an outage at night stops therapy and many machines will not restart until you notice and press a button.

Switchover speed is the spec to look for. EcoFlow rates the River 3 Plus and Delta 3 Plus EPS modes at 10 milliseconds or less, which is within the range most electronics tolerate. Not every power station offers a true UPS function, and some that offer pass-through charging have a noticeable gap during switchover, so check the current spec sheet for a stated switchover time before you buy for this purpose. A traditional computer UPS also works for this role, and our guide to the [best UPS battery backups](/best-ups-battery-backup/) covers those, but most office UPS units are designed for a few minutes of runtime, not a whole night.

Leaving a station permanently plugged in raises reasonable questions about battery wear. LFP chemistry, which every station on this list uses, tolerates being held at a high state of charge much better than older lithium chemistries, and several brands let you set a charge limit in the app. Setting the limit to around 80 to 90 percent for a bedside UPS is a sensible compromise if you do not expect long outages, though it trims your runtime accordingly.

Noise is the other bedside consideration. A station charging fast spins up its cooling fans, and a fan cycling on at 2 a.m. can be more disruptive than the CPAP. Most of the time, a station in pass-through mode with a full battery is quiet, but after an outage it will recharge when the grid returns. If your station lets you set a slower AC charge rate, use it for a bedroom unit.

sections.heading: Comparison Table: Capacity, Output and Best Use
sections.body:
Here is how the seven picks line up on the specs that matter for a CPAP. Capacities and outputs are the manufacturers' published ratings; the nights estimate uses the DC, humidifier-off planning figure of 25 watts from the runtime section, and should be treated as a rough guide only. Turn on heated humidification and divide by two or more.

| Product | Capacity / output | Rough nights (DC, 25W) | Flies? | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| EcoFlow River 3 Plus | 286Wh / 600W | About 1 | No | All-rounder, bedside UPS |
| Medistrom Pilot-24 Lite | 99Wh / DC only | Under 1 at 25W; more at low pressure | Yes, no approval needed | Air travel, backpacking |
| Jackery Explorer 300 Plus | 288Wh / 300W | About 1 | No | Light camping |
| Anker SOLIX C300 | 288Wh / 300W | About 1 | No | CPAP plus laptop |
| Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 | 1,070Wh / 1,500W | 4+ | No | Multi-night outages |
| EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus | 1,024Wh / 1,800W | 4+ | No | Bedside UPS for long outages |
| Honda EU2200i | Gas, 1,800W running | Fuel-limited | No | Daytime recharging |

The pattern is clear. The 286-288Wh class is the right size for one night with margin and is light enough to carry anywhere you can drive. The kilowatt-hour class is a different kind of purchase, sized for a household outage rather than a CPAP alone, and it makes sense if you were going to buy a home-backup battery anyway. If you are weighing brands within those classes, our [EcoFlow vs Jackery comparison](/ecoflow-vs-jackery/), plus the brand roundups for [EcoFlow](/best-ecoflow-power-station/) and [Jackery](/best-jackery-power-station/), go deeper on the differences.

What the table does not show is that dedicated CPAP batteries and power stations solve different problems. The Pilot-24 Lite is the only option here you can take on a plane, and it is the lightest, but it has the least capacity per dollar. The power stations are cheaper per watt-hour, run other devices, and recharge from solar, but they are bigger and cannot fly. Many CPAP users end up owning one of each.

sections.heading: Which CPAP Battery to Buy
sections.body:
If you want one battery that handles a power outage at home and a weekend camping trip, buy the EcoFlow River 3 Plus. It is the right capacity for a night with a DC cable, its fast EPS mode makes it a real bedside backup, and the optional extra battery lets it grow into a multi-night unit later. The Jackery Explorer 300 Plus is the simpler alternative if you do not need UPS function and value a light, uncomplicated box.

If you fly, buy the Medistrom Pilot-24 Lite, or the Pilot-12 Lite if your machine is a 12V model, and confirm the cable for your exact CPAP. For a two-night trip, buy two. If your CPAP travels with a laptop, phone and tablet that all need charging, the Anker SOLIX C300 makes the most of a small station's USB-C output.

If you live where outages last days, step up to a kilowatt-hour station. Pick the EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus if a seamless bedside UPS is the priority and you may expand it later; pick the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 if you want the lightest 1kWh box. Either will also run a refrigerator during the day, and our guides to the [best home battery backup](/best-home-battery-backup/) and [power stations for home backup](/best-portable-power-station-for-home-backup/) cover bigger systems if you want whole-room coverage.

And if you already own a generator or are shopping for the best generator for a CPAP machine, buy a quiet inverter model like the Honda EU2200i and use it to recharge a battery during the day, not to run the CPAP overnight. Our [home generator guide](/best-home-generator-for-power-outages/) covers larger units for whole-house needs. Whatever you buy, test it on a normal night before you need it, and confirm the DC cable and settings with your CPAP manufacturer or DME supplier.

mistakes.title: Sizing the battery from the power brick label
mistakes.body: The 90-watt rating on many CPAP power supplies is the maximum, not the average. Sizing from it overestimates draw and can push you toward a heavier battery than you need. Measure real overnight use with a plug-in watt meter, once with the humidifier on and once with it off.

mistakes.title: Forgetting the humidifier doubles the draw
mistakes.body: Heated humidification and heated tubing can turn a 25-watt machine into a 60-watt one, especially in a cold room. A battery that covers two humidifier-free nights may not last one with everything on. Decide which settings you will use on battery nights first, ideally after measuring both, then buy a battery sized for them.

mistakes.title: Buying the wrong voltage cable
mistakes.body: ResMed AirSense machines run on 24V, other brands on 12V, and battery makers sell different packs and cables for each. A 12V pack with a 24V machine will not work. Check your exact model on the battery maker's compatibility chart, or ask your DME supplier, before ordering.

mistakes.title: Trying to fly with a power station
mistakes.body: Lithium batteries over 160 watt-hours are not allowed on passenger aircraft, and stations in the 286-288Wh class exceed that. Medical need does not change the rule. Pack a sub-100Wh dedicated CPAP battery in your carry-on for flights, confirm your airline's policy in advance, and leave the power station at home for outages and drive-in camping.

mistakes.title: Running a generator indoors or near a tent
mistakes.body: A generator, or an idling car, produces carbon monoxide that can kill a sleeping person. Never run either in a garage, tent or near open windows. Run the generator outdoors by day to recharge a battery, and let the battery power the CPAP silently overnight.

faqs.q: What is the best battery backup for a CPAP?
faqs.a: For most people, a roughly 300 watt-hour LFP power station like the EcoFlow River 3 Plus, used with a DC cable, is the best all-round choice. It covers about a night with the humidifier off, works as a bedside backup, and doubles as a camping battery. Frequent flyers should add a sub-100Wh dedicated pack like the Medistrom Pilot-24 Lite.

faqs.q: How long will a battery run a CPAP?
faqs.a: Divide the battery's watt-hours, times about 0.9 on DC or 0.85 on AC, by your machine's average watts. A 288Wh station on DC with a 25-watt draw gives roughly 10 hours. Turn on a heated humidifier and the same battery may give only about 4 hours. Measure your machine's real draw with a watt meter for an accurate answer.

faqs.q: Can I run my CPAP from a power station's AC outlet?
faqs.a: Yes. Every station here has a pure sine wave inverter that can run a CPAP's standard power brick. The trade-off is efficiency: the inverter wastes energy, so you get less runtime than with a DC converter from the 12V port. Use AC if your machine needs it for heated humidification, and confirm the setup with your CPAP manufacturer.

faqs.q: What size CPAP battery can I take on a plane?
faqs.a: Under FAA rules for passengers, spare lithium batteries go in carry-on only. Batteries of 100Wh or less are generally allowed without approval; 100 to 160Wh need airline approval and are usually limited to two; anything over 160Wh is prohibited. Check your airline's own medical-device policy too, since carriers can be stricter.

faqs.q: What is the best generator for a CPAP machine?
faqs.a: A quiet inverter generator such as the Honda EU2200i, used outdoors to recharge a power station during the day. Inverter output suits sensitive electronics. Running a generator all night just for a CPAP wastes fuel, disturbs neighbors and puts a carbon monoxide source near sleeping people, so let a battery run the machine overnight.

faqs.q: Will a CPAP restart by itself after a power outage?
faqs.a: It depends on the machine and settings. Some CPAPs resume therapy when power returns, others wait for you to press start, and many users only discover the answer during an outage. A power station with a fast UPS or EPS mode avoids the question by keeping the machine running through the outage. Check your manual or ask your DME supplier.

faqs.q: Is a power station a medical device?
faqs.a: No. The power stations in this guide are general-purpose consumer batteries and are not medically certified. They supply power to your CPAP the same way a wall outlet does. Your CPAP manufacturer lists approved power accessories, and your doctor and DME supplier should confirm any battery setup before you rely on it for therapy.

bottomLine:
Size a CPAP battery for the settings you will actually sleep with on battery power. With the humidifier off and a DC cable, a roughly 300Wh station like the EcoFlow River 3 Plus covers a night with margin and makes an excellent bedside backup.

Fly with a sub-100Wh dedicated pack like the Medistrom Pilot-24 Lite, step up to a 1kWh station for multi-day outages, and keep any generator outdoors and charging batteries by day. Confirm every cable and setting with your CPAP maker, DME supplier and doctor.
